chapter: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
title: Will Roland and Charlie Parker's courtesy
summary: Showman Will Roland, who couldn't play, pushed Parker aside at the Jungle Room; Parker listened politely, since 'everybody's got something'.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: [LAUGHS] You know, we used to play at Jack's Basket Room and the different places, playing after-hours sets. But across from the Lincoln Theatre was a place called the Jungle Room. And the house band was led by a fellow named Will Roland. And he always worked two jobs; he

worked before-hours and after-hours. And he had his big car, and he dressed, he was real dapper and everything. And the guy knew nothing about the saxophone, but he was one of the busiest guys in town. All he would do was blow into the horn and just work his fingers, and bow his body up and down to whatever was... Everything meant the same to him, you know.
And all the guys would be in. Billy Eckstine. And Gerry Gray, Wardell's wife, would be there. They used to really put him on, you know.

And so, I'll never forget the first night he heard Charlie Parker. He had been hearing about Charlie Parker, that Charlie Parker was in town, and everybody was laying for him to walk in because Charlie Parker was on the stand. So we were up on the stand, and Charlie Parker was right in the middle of his solo playing "Cherokee." And when Will Roland came in, he headed straight for the bandstand. You know, he wanted to get to Charlie Parker, you know. And Billy Eckstine was eggin' him on. "Hey, Roland, all right, Roland, go on in and get it!" You know, he was loud, talkin' all the way across the room! [LAUGHS]
Will Roland came up, pulled his saxophone out, and pushed Charlie Parker away from the microphone, and started bowin' and duckin', bowin'...goin' through his act -- and

broke it up. That's to let you know how people's minds were, you know. And he didn't know anything about the saxophone. And Charlie Parker just politely moved away and let him have it, and looked around in amazement -- because he didn't know anything about Roland either! And do you know, he stood there and listened to Roland play?

On another occasion, I saw him do this to a guy at Billy Berg's when we were playing at a jam session one Sunday. This guy came up, he was a horrible saxophone player. And when he played, Charlie Parker gave him the same attention he gave everybody else -- he just stood there and listened. So later on, the tenor player, Gene Montgomery, said, "Bird, you know you're not enjoying it." And he said, "Well, look, man, everybody's got something." I never forgot that, you know. He said, "Everybody's got something." As bad as he sounded, he had something.

Oh, he went back to Oklahoma (he was from Oklahoma) when things fell apart out here. But he was a big man in Los Angeles, you know. Because he was a showman, you know. He had his boot (?) and he was dressed, he was sharp all the time, and he'd be going through all these motions, acting like he's playing, you know. And I think he really believed himself after so long!
